turns.question: You said the repository saves the intent to the local database before sending. On Android, what exactly goes into that intent record, and how do you make sure it's durable before the network call starts?

card.adopted: MVP path: send money to a saved contact, confirmed on a native screen, with a server ledger and failure handling

more: The intent record holds the client transfer ID, the payer account, the recipient, the amount as a Long in minor units (8000 cents), the currency, and a status of pending. card.problem: Design a mobile wallet from scratch, including the system behind it and how it handles failures
card.adopted: MVP path: send money to a saved contact, confirmed on a native screen, with a server ledger and failure handling
card.constraints: ["Balance held by the wallet itself, one currency for the MVP, offline only for reading the last known balance (assumptions to confirm)", "Balance held by the wallet server ledger, not the phone; the phone shows the last known balance", "Payment can start from a group chat, but the user picks the recipient and amount on a trusted native confirmation; the server binds the authorization to payer, recipient, amount and expiry", "If the chat stream drops after confirm, the app reads the status from the payment service by the same client transfer ID"]
card.abandoned: ["MVP path: send money to a saved contact, confirmed on a native screen, with a real ledger and failure handling"]
card.heard: Chat entry with two Alexes and no reliable amount; stream drops after confirm
card.say: Two things change. The chat only suggests a payment, so the user picks the right Alex and the amount on a native confirm screen. transcript: Interviewer: Hi, I'm the founder of ActAI. We're building an agent-first mobile communication app, focused on how people talk, coordinate and work together every day. Today we'll start with a project you really owned, then design a fictional mobile wallet together. I'll add a few new conditions along the way, and leave time for your questions at the end.
Interviewer: Pick the one project that best shows your mobile skills. Who used it, what problem did it solve, and where did your responsibility start and end?
Candidate: The users were travelers on the KKday app.
Candidate: They wanted a trip they could book, but planning by hand took a lot of time.
Candidate: They had to work out the budget, search products one by one, and put the plan together.
Candidate: So the AI took a destination, a budget and a number of days, and built a bookable plan.
Candidate: My responsibility started at the technical plan: the agent design, the product and order tools, and the core backend.
Candidate: It ended at the app side, where I wrote the code that reads the streamed plan.
Candidate: The app team built the screens; the agent and backend were mine.
Candidate: After launch, the system handled about 300,000 trip planning requests a day.

Interviewer: On the KKday trip planner, you said the agent and backend were yours while the app team built the screens. Walk me through the streamed-plan reading code you wrote on the app side — what exactly did you build there versus what the app team owned?
Candidate: On the app side, I wrote the code that opens the SSE connection and reads the stream.
Candidate: Each event carries one piece of the plan, like a day card or a product card.
Candidate: I parse it and push it into a StateFlow, so the screen shows Day 1 while the rest is still coming.
Candidate: The app team owned the screens and the card layouts.
Candidate: I owned the stream reading, the parsing and the fallback when an event is broken.
Candidate: Retries were capped at two attempts, so a persistently failing part falls back to a placeholder card instead of blocking the rest of the plan.
Interviewer: Pick a change you personally made. Walk me from one user action through the UI, data or network path. Which logic did you actually change?
Candidate: The change I made was in the SKU calculation on the product page.
Candidate: Before, every tap on an option recalculated all the price and stock combinations on the main thread.
Candidate: So I flattened the configuration and built a price and stock index once, ahead of time.
Candidate: Then a tap just looked up the result, and the heavy work moved to Dispatchers.Default.
Candidate: Results came back through StateFlow, so the screen updated without freezing.
Candidate: The index is rebuilt only when the product's option set changes, so a stale index can't be served after an edit.
Interviewer: What was the hardest bug to reproduce there? What did you suspect first, and which log, experiment or repro proved you wrong?
Candidate: The hardest bug was a stale price after a merchant edited a product.
Candidate: I suspected the index first, because it was built once and cached in memory.
Candidate: My first guess was wrong: the index was fine.
Candidate: I added a log of the option-set version and the index version, and the log showed the app kept the old index after the edit.
Candidate: So I rebuilt the index when the option set changed, and the bug was gone.

Candidate: Rebuilding on every edit can be costly for a large catalog, so I'd rebuild lazily on the next read or debounce it, and add a test that edits a product then checks the price so a stale index can't return.

Interviewer: You said the log showed the app kept the old index after the edit — how did you confirm that version mismatch was actually the cause of the stale price, rather than just a correlation you noticed?
Candidate: Right, the version log showed the cause, not just a pattern.
Candidate: The app read the old index after the edit, so the version check is what proved it.
Candidate: I'd keep that check in the code, so a mismatch is caught early.
Interviewer: What other options did you have, why didn't you pick them, and after release how did you know the change worked?
Candidate: There were two other options.
Candidate: First, I could rebuild the index on every edit.
Candidate: Second, I could skip the index and calculate on each tap.
Candidate: I didn't pick the first because a large catalog makes every edit expensive.
Candidate: I didn't pick the second because that was the slow path I was fixing.
Candidate: For the release, I checked it myself by editing a product and going through the booking flow.
Candidate: I didn't pick the second one because that was the slow path I was fixing.
Candidate: For the release, I checked it myself by editing a product and going through the booking flow.
Candidate: I didn't have timing logs or user data, so that check was my own, not a measured result.

Interviewer: Tell me about a time you saw a delivery risk or a likely delay and the team disagreed. When did you tell whom, how many options did you give, who decided, and what did you finish yourself?
Candidate: I told the project manager the same day I found it.
Candidate: I hadn't checked every page yet, but it could already affect that week's release.
Candidate: I gave two options.
Candidate: One, ship the old pages and move my change to the next release.
Candidate: Two, ship it this week and accept the risk of untested pages.
Candidate: He decided, and he chose to keep the old pages.
Candidate: Everything else shipped on time.
Candidate: I finished the fix and the testing myself, and my change went out in the next release.
Interviewer: You said you'd ship this week and accept the risk of untested pages — what specific risk were you willing to accept there, and who was watching the data after release?
Candidate: The risk was the back button.
Candidate: On some old pages it jumped straight to the home screen instead of the stock details.
Candidate: Two pages were affected, and I hadn't checked the rest yet.
Candidate: So shipping that week meant users could hit a broken back button on pages we hadn't tested.
Candidate: I wasn't willing to accept that, which is why I gave the option to keep the old pages.

Interviewer: Let's switch to the design exercise. Design a mobile wallet from scratch: the core mobile experience, the system behind it, and how it handles failures. Start by clarifying the requirements. Which user path would you define as the MVP?
Candidate: Good morning.
Candidate: Before I design, a few questions.
Candidate: Is the balance held by us, or does money move on a bank or card rail?
Candidate: Which currencies do we support?
Candidate: What should work offline?
Candidate: Does that match what you want?
Candidate: I'd cap the MVP at one currency and one payment rail, and treat offline mode as read-only, so the ledger never has to reconcile conflicting writes from a device that was out of sync.

Interviewer: Here are the rules: signed-in users, centralized balance accounts, single currency USD, internal peer-to-peer transfers, zero fees. Balance, transfer, history and details are in scope. Cached reads work offline; submitting money needs the network. The server owns the authoritative ledger and limits. Top-up, withdrawal and multi-currency are out of scope. A has 100 dollars and B has zero. Draw the client, the server and local storage as a flowchart, and tell me what each part owns.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the three parts and the send flow.
Candidate: The phone owns the screens and the last known balance.
Candidate: The server owns the ledger, and it's the only place money moves.
Candidate: The local database keeps the cached balance and the transfer intent, saved before we send.
Candidate: A has 100 dollars, so 10000 cents, and B has 0.

Candidate: The client transfer ID is generated on the phone, so the server must treat it as untrusted and scope it per account; otherwise a replayed ID from another user could return someone else's result.
Interviewer: Now draw a sequence diagram of A sending B 80 dollars: confirmation, request, ledger and the result screen.
Candidate: Okay, I'll draw the send sequence.
Candidate: The screen saves the intent to the local database first.
Candidate: Then the repository sends it to the server with the client transfer ID.
Candidate: The server checks and moves the money in one transaction, then returns the result.
Candidate: The repository saves that result and the ViewModel shows it.

Candidate: The screen shows success only from the server's record, never from the local save.

Interviewer: You said the repository saves the intent to the local database before sending. On Android, what exactly goes into that intent record, and how do you make sure it's durable before the network call starts?
Candidate: The client ID is made on the phone, so the server must treat it as untrusted and scope it per account; otherwise a replayed ID from another user could return someone else's result.
Candidate: The intent record holds the client transfer ID, the payer account, the recipient, the amount as a Long in minor units (8000 cents), the currency, and a status of pending.
Candidate: I save it in Room with a suspend insert, and I only start the network call after that insert returns.
Candidate: Room writes to disk in a transaction, so the row is on disk before the POST goes out.
Candidate: If the app dies right after the insert, the row is still there on restart.

Interviewer: Your sequence assumes the response comes back and the repository saves the result, but if the server commits and the response is lost before Android kills the process, A reopens with only a pending intent. What does A see on the balance and history screens, and how does the app resolve that pending intent? Please update your sequence diagram.
Candidate: A's balance stays at 10000 cents, because the phone only shows the last balance the server confirmed.
Candidate: The pending intent is not proof that money moved, so the app doesn't guess.
Candidate: On the next launch, the repository finds the pending row and asks the server for its status by account and client transfer ID.
Candidate: If the server has the transfer, the app saves that status and shows the real balance.
Candidate: If the lookup finds nothing, the state stays unknown, because the request may still be in flight.

Interviewer: You said if the lookup finds nothing the state stays unknown because the request may still be in flight — but what stops the user from just tapping send again while that pending row sits there, and how does your UI actually prevent a second transfer to B?
